title: Taking refuge formally
hookLine: many take the three refuges and five precepts before a monk or teacher

lines: A WOMAN KNEELS BEFORE A MONK.
cards: In a temple hall, a young woman kneels in front of an older monk. Her family sits behind her. The monk says a line in Pali, and she repeats it.
Then the next. Three lines, then the same three again, and a third time. Then five short promises.
It takes about three minutes. Nothing flashes, nobody cries, and afterward there's tea. But she will remember this morning for the rest of her life.

teach.b: Here are the lines, in the Pali that Theravada Buddhists use: "Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi. Dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi. Saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi." I go to the Buddha for refuge. I go to the teaching for refuge.
I go to the community for refuge. Then again, with the word for second time, and again with the word for third time. Saying it three times marks it as meant.

Then the five precepts, each worded as a training rule: I undertake the training to refrain from taking life, from taking what isn't given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from intoxicants that cloud the mind.
You met each of them in the practices camp.

teach.h: SARANA — A SHELTER IN A STORM.
teach.b: Saraṇa means shelter, the place you run to in a storm. So refuge isn't joining a club or signing a creed. It's saying out loud where you turn when things get hard.
In the Theravada, people often repeat the refuges and precepts after a monk at many temple gatherings, again and again through life.
In Tibetan communities there's a refuge ceremony with a lama, sometimes a tiny snip of hair, and a refuge name.
In Zen, a ceremony of receiving the precepts may include a dharma name and a small sewn robe worn around the neck. And almost every teacher says the same thing: there's no rush.
Some people take refuge in their first month. Some never do, and practice for decades. The door stays open.

how: Theravada Buddhists commonly repeat the three refuges and five precepts after a monk at temple gatherings; in Tibetan communities people take refuge from a lama and often receive a refuge name; in Zen a precepts ceremony (jukai) may include a dharma name and a small robe.

o: five vows that only ordained monks may take
five commands to obey without question
five training rules, taken up with the refuges

games.q: match the pieces of taking refuge.

s: taking refuge is like signing a creed
it's saying where you turn when things are hard: the Buddha, the teaching, the community.
in the Theravada, people often repeat the refuges many times through life
at many temple gatherings, after a monk.
you have to take refuge within your first year of practice
teachers say there's no rush; some never do and practice for decades.

games.q: you've practiced for a year. a teacher mentions a refuge ceremony next month. you're honestly not sure. what do most teachers say?
o: decide now, or the chance is gone.
take your time; the door stays open.
games.why: almost every teacher says there's no rush. some take refuge early, some never do, and the door stays open.

practice: Sit beside one question without deciding anything: someday, would you want to take refuge formally?

Yes, no and I don't know are all fine answers, so just notice what comes up, curiosity, hesitation, warmth or nothing at all, and don't argue with it. Then let the question rest, and come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Five precepts. The five training rules taken up, along with the three refuges, by anyone who formally takes refuge before a monk or teacher.

orig.note: Pali saraṇa: shelter, refuge, as in Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, I go to the Buddha for refuge.

carryVoice: Your line: when you're ready. Where you already turn when things go wrong is a first answer to what refuge means for you. Day three hundred twenty-three, done.
